lead: A beam resting on a wall and a roller looks simple, but the wall and the roller are not part of the beam. To apply equilibrium you must first cut the beam free: draw it alone and replace each support by the force it can exert. That drawing is a free body diagram, or FBD. Its reactions are the numbers a beam design starts from: the load a wall bracket must take, the push a bridge bearing sends into a pier. This chapter gives the steps, the two or three equilibrium equations, and the order that finds the reactions with the least algebra.
prereq: You need: 3.1 for the standard support and load types, and first-year statics for resolving forces and taking moments about a point.

sections.h3: Cut the beam free, then put back only forces

blocks.text: A beam sitting on a wall and a roller is not a free body. The wall pushes on it. The roller pushes on it. The equations ΣF = 0 and ΣM = 0 hold only for a body with every contact removed and every removed contact replaced by a force. So the first job is to cut the beam free.

items: Draw the beam alone as a single line, at its true length, to scale if you can.
Erase the supports, the wall, the floor and any hanger. Nothing touches the beam now.
At each support draw the reaction that support can give. If you do not know its direction, assume upward and let a minus sign in the answer correct you.

Replace each distributed load by one resultant. A UDL of w over length L becomes wL acting at mid-length. A triangular load rising to w over length L becomes wL/2, acting at one-third of L from the tall end.
Keep every point load where it is, and mark its distance from one chosen end.

blocks.text: Now the beam is a free body carrying a few unknown arrows, and only those unknowns are missing. Every other number on the drawing is known.

A support can give only the forces its construction allows. A roller on a floor cannot pull the beam down, so it gives one force normal to the floor, usually vertical. A pin can push in any direction in the plane, so it gives two components, usually one horizontal and one vertical. A fixed end also resists rotation, so it gives a moment as well.

head: Support
Reaction you draw
Unknowns
rows: Roller, or a beam end free to slide
One force normal to the surface

blocks.text: Count the unknowns before you write any equation. A plane beam with three or fewer unknown reactions is statically determinate: the three equilibrium equations are enough to find them all. A beam with more than three unknowns is statically indeterminate, and equilibrium alone cannot finish the job; that case waits for Unit 5, Deflection of Beams and Energy Methods.

Fix the signs first and keep them. Take upward as positive for forces, and anticlockwise as positive for moments. A force F whose line of action is at perpendicular distance d from the moment centre gives the moment F·d. A force whose line of action passes through the centre gives zero moment.
ΣFx = 0,   ΣFy = 0,   ΣM = 0 about any point
blocks.where: ΣFx is the sum of horizontal force components in N or kN; ΣFy is the sum of vertical components; ΣM is the sum of moments in N·m or kN·m about any chosen point in the plane of the beam.

items: Take moments about one support, say A. The reaction at A passes through A, so its moment is zero and it drops out.
Solve that single equation for the reaction at the other support, B.
Use ΣFy = 0 to get the reaction at A.
Check with a moment equation about B. It must give the same R_A.
Use ΣFx = 0 only if a horizontal load exists; with all loads vertical, the horizontal reaction at a pin is zero.

blocks.text: The order matters because it turns three simultaneous equations into one equation, then one substitution. Taking moments about an arbitrary point leaves both unknowns in the equation and costs time for no gain.

figure.caption: The flow from a supported beam to two known reactions. Notice that the UDL becomes a single 30 kN force at mid-length, 3 m from A, and that the last box is a check, not a new calculation.

spec.title: Reactions in five moves
spec.aria: A downward flow from isolating the beam, replacing the supports by reactions, replacing the UDL by 30 kilonewtons at mid-length, taking moments about A, summing vertical forces, and checking with a moment about B.

examples.question: A simply supported beam AB is 6 m long. A is a pin, B is a roller on a horizontal floor. A point load of 20 kN acts 2 m from A, and a UDL of 5 kN/m covers the whole span. Draw the free body diagram and find both reactions.
steps: Free body diagram: beam line AB, 6 m long. Draw R_A vertically upward at A, R_B vertically upward at B. No horizontal load acts, so the horizontal component at the pin is zero.
Replace the UDL: wL = 5 × 6 = 30 kN, acting at mid-length, that is 3 m from A.
Take moments about A, anticlockwise positive: R_B × 6 − 20 × 2 − 30 × 3 = 0.
Check by moments about B: 20 × 4 + 30 × 3 = 80 + 90 = 170 kN·m, and R_A × 6 = 28.33 × 6 = 170 kN·m. Equal, so the answers are consistent.
Check total force: downward 20 + 30 = 50 kN; upward 28.33 + 21.67 = 50 kN. R_A is larger because the 20 kN load sits nearer A.
examples.answer: R_A = 28.33 kN upward and R_B = 21.67 kN upward.
examples.check:
P = 20.0
a = 2.0
L = 6.0
w = 5.0
W = w * L
RB = (P * a + W * (L / 2)) / L
RA = P + W - RB
print(round(RB, 2))
print(round(RA, 2))
print(round(RA * L, 2))

traps: Putting the resultant of a UDL at a support or at the end of the beam. For a UDL over the whole span it sits at mid-length, 3 m from A in this beam, never at A.
Writing the UDL as w instead of wL. A 5 kN/m load over 6 m is 30 kN in total, not 5 kN.
Stopping after the moment equation. That gives one reaction only; R_A needs the ΣFy step, and examiners take a mark for it.
Switching sign convention halfway. A moment written clockwise-positive in one line and anticlockwise-positive in the next gives a reaction that is right in size and wrong in sign.
Adding a horizontal reaction when every load is vertical. A roller on a horizontal floor gives only a vertical force, and the pin's horizontal component is zero here.

quiz.q: What is a free body diagram?
quiz.a: A drawing of one body alone, with every support, wall and contact removed, and each removed contact replaced by the force or moment it exerted on the body.

quiz.q: How many unknown reactions does a roller on a horizontal floor give, and in which direction?
quiz.a: One, acting normal to the floor, that is vertically upward. It cannot resist sliding along the floor or rotation.

quiz.q: Why is the first moment equation taken about a support rather than an arbitrary point on the beam?
quiz.a: The reaction at that support passes through the moment centre, so its moment arm is zero and it drops out. One equation then holds one unknown, and the rest is substitution instead of solving simultaneous equations.

quiz.q: A simply supported beam of span 4 m carries only a UDL of 8 kN/m over the whole span. Find both reactions.
quiz.a: Resultant wL = 8 × 4 = 32 kN at mid-length, 2 m from either end. By symmetry each reaction is 32 ÷ 2 = 16 kN upward. Check: ΣM about A gives R_B × 4 = 32 × 2 = 64, so R_B = 16 kN.

quiz.q: A 5 m beam is pinned at A and on a roller at B. A point load of 30 kN acts 2 m from A. Find R_A and R_B.
quiz.a: ΣM about A: R_B × 5 = 30 × 2 = 60, so R_B = 12 kN. ΣFy: R_A = 30 − 12 = 18 kN. Check about B: 30 × 3 = 90 and 18 × 5 = 90, equal.

quiz.q: A cantilever is fixed at A and free at B, with a UDL over its length. Count the unknowns and say whether the beam is statically determinate.
quiz.a: The fixed end gives three unknowns: a horizontal force, a vertical force and a moment. The three equilibrium equations are exactly enough, so the beam is statically determinate and the reactions can be found by the same method; the shear force and bending moment diagrams follow in 3.3.

quiz.q: Two students get R_A = 28.33 kN and R_B = 21.67 kN for the 6 m beam. One checks ΣFy = 0 and stops. The other also takes moments about B. Which check is stronger and why?
quiz.a: The moment check about B is stronger. R_A came from ΣFy, so ΣFy will always balance whatever mistakes were made earlier; it is not an independent test. The moment equation about B was not used in the solution, so it independently confirms both numbers.

beyond: Not for the exam. In design offices the reactions of a real beam are found by frame analysis software, but the free body diagram is still the thing engineers sketch to check the output. Influence lines go one step further: they show how a reaction changes as a rolling load, such as a train on a bridge girder, moves across the span. Search for 'influence line for reaction' and 'bearing reaction of a bridge girder' to see the same three equations applied to moving loads.
